A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IP-SAM research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2 adds readable Appendices A–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original COD experiments, component and design ablations, and medical polyp segmentation results in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds IP-SAM results on salient object detection, conditioning ablations, runtime measurements and qualitative failure analysis. Quoted competitor scores in Table 5 are distinguished from the authors' results.

M1.justification: The SPG, frozen prompt encoder, PSG, residual anchoring, propagated mask tokens, decoder, LoRA adaptation and training losses remain unchanged. Appendix A explicitly uses the same architecture for SOD; the new ablation variants do not revise the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix A adds standard RGB salient object detection, training on DUTS-TR and evaluating on DUTS-TE, DUT-OMRON, HKU-IS, ECSSD and PASCAL-S. This extends coverage beyond the retained COD and medical polyp tasks.

E2.justification: Table 5 introduces a substantial SOD comparator set, including F3Net, GateNet-X, Samba, VSCode-S, SAM2-UNet and SAM2-LPNet, alongside retained SAM adaptations. Available competitor scores are quoted from their papers. Tables 1 and 4 retain their comparator membership; Figure 6 additionally includes MedSAM in the polyp qualitative comparison.

E3.justification: The added SOD evaluation uses maximum F-measure and maximum E-measure and includes published competitor results. Appendix E introduces controls sharing decoder architecture, initialization and training recipe, with specified prompt-input transformations. Appendix F adds synchronized CUDA-event profiling. The existing COD and polyp training protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component and design ablations, Table 6 reports controlled null-prompt and encoder-bypass comparisons and explicit sigmoid, binarization and logit-scaling analyses. Tables 7 and Figures 5–8 add runtime decomposition, qualitative case studies and internal visualizations of failure cases.

E5.justification: Table 7(b) newly reports timing variability and averaging over 200 runs after 50 warm-up iterations. Both versions already report three-seed averaging and COD10K MAE of 0.017 ± 0.001; no increase in accuracy-evaluation run counts is documented.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes CAMO MAE for Minimal-SPG direct output from 0.028 to 0.058 and Minimal-SPG + PromptSpace from 0.019 to 0.049, without explaining the revisions. Tables 1, 2 and 4 retain their numerical results. Tables 5–7 add SOD scores, conditioning/logit results and component timings, while Figures 5–8 add qualitative outcomes.

T1.justification: The method equations, mathematical definitions and loss formulation are retained. The appendix adds empirical analyses and interpretive discussion, without new theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: Despite the broader title and shortened abstract, the main claims remain prompt-space conditioning without external prompts, asymmetric background suppression, strong COD performance with 21.26M trainable parameters and transfer to medical segmentation. The SOD evaluation supplies additional evidence for the existing generalization claim.

C2.justification: Appendices E–H substantially expand interpretation of conditioning pathways, logit formats and computational overhead. The brief existing over-suppression limitation becomes a detailed account of truncation, topological fracture and missing instances. The appendix also limits the evidence to foreground-background segmentation and identifies broader semantic and complex multi-instance segmentation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds reproducibility details for the appendix controls, including the approximately 34K-parameter bypass projection, zero dense embeddings, binarization threshold and logit multipliers. It also documents wall-clock versus CUDA-event timing procedures. The main architecture specifications, training hyperparameters, hardware and LoRA settings are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially broadens the comparison literature to SOD specialists and additional SAM adaptations. Nineteen works are added, covering the new methods and benchmark sources, increasing the bibliography from 38 to 57 entries. Section 2's original positioning relative to feature adaptation and automatic prompting remains intact.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, condenses the abstract, adds keywords, replaces placeholder running headers and clarifies Table 3 terminology. It appends a claim-and-evidence roadmap and sections A–H, while retaining nearly all main-text prose and section ordering.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–7 and Figures 5–8, providing new benchmark, ablation, runtime and qualitative displays. Figures 1–4 are retained. Table 3 moves below its discussion and receives revised labels and notes; the document also gains a boxed abstract and wider page margins.

improvement.justification: The fixed-decoder controls and quantified logit-format analyses in Table 6 substantially strengthen evidence attributing gains to prompt conditioning. The SOD evaluation and explicit failure visualizations also better substantiate generalization and define its limits beyond v1's brief limitations discussion. Quoted SOD baselines limit comparison fairness, and the retained speed claim requires caution given the higher synchronized timings in Table 7, but the added controlled evidence and failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.
